prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength brought optical time and frequency measurement to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize to Katori and Ye for the optical lattice clock. Round 1 sharpened my reasons rather than changing them. The core experimental facts are not disputed by anyone: trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength cancels the light shift, which gives a very large atom number and therefore a statistical advantage that single-ion clocks cannot match, and independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) have compared their clocks and agree at the 1e-18 level. That kind of cross-checked agreement is the evidence I weigh most. Danielsson is right that the citation should not rest on precision alone, and I now accept that the wording should name the mechanism (magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms) and the demonstrated accuracy, and leave the downstream uses out of the text. Those uses, redshift tests across millimetres and many-body clock physics, are actual results and can be mentioned in the committee's popular and scientific background, whereas geodesy and dark-matter searches are still prospects. Six of eight members now prefer this entry, but I do not treat the count as the argument. The argument is that this is the one shortlisted case where the discovery, the credit and the independent verification are all in hand at the same time.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion control) is the objection everyone repeats, and I do not think it is empty. I answer it as an experimentalist: the comb is a ruler and ion control is single-particle quantum control, whereas the lattice clock is a different physical regime in which many atoms are held without Doppler or recoil shifts and the light shift is engineered to vanish. Neither earlier prize covers that. Still, Ye's own laser-stabilisation and comb work sits close to 2005, so the citation must be anchored on the lattice clock. Two further weaknesses remain. First, Olsson's question about Ye's role is fair: the magic-wavelength concept is Katori's, and Ye's contribution is the demonstration of record accuracy, stability and the many-body clock physics, which is decisive development rather than original invention, and the citation wording 'invention and development' covers both without claiming that Ye conceived the scheme. Second, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Derevianko are outside the credit, which is the unavoidable price of the three-name limit and is far smaller than the gaps in B057. The SI second has not been redefined yet; I treat that as confirmation to come, not a condition for the science.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the citation rest on demonstrated accuracy and comparisons rather than on geodesy and dark-matter searches, which are promises, and asks whether the two-name configuration holds if Ye's role is development of Katori's concept rather than invention.
responses.response: I agree on the first point and have changed my text because of it: my round-1 case leaned on geodesy and dark-matter searches, and the proposed citation now mentions only the trapping mechanism and the measured 1e-18 level. Redshift tests over millimetres and many-body effects in the lattice are results, so they can go in the background document. On the second point, Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is the original idea and his is the firmest name. Ye's contribution is the strontium clock taken to record accuracy and stability, and the first control of spin-exchange and many-body effects in the lattice. From the lab side that is not secondary: without a clock that works at 1e-18 the idea would still be a proposal. I hold the pair as invention (Katori) plus decisive development (Ye), and I do not think a third name, Takamoto for the first Sr demonstration or Lemonde, is needed to make the pair defensible. I would not sacrifice the clean two-name credit for it.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B027 and wants the citation to rest on what the precision has shown, redshift tests at millimetre scale and many-body clock physics, so it does not read as a third award for better clocks after 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I accept this in part. The risk of reading as better clocks again is real, and the citation should say invention and name magic-wavelength trapping. I would stop short of putting redshift tests in the citation itself: the millimetre-scale redshift measurement is a single demonstration, still limited by clock comparison and not by a new theory test, while the 1e-18 level itself is established by many independent comparisons. Quoting the precision keeps the citation tied to what has been verified, and the scientific background can then say what that precision has already shown, as Danielsson wishes. I also thank him for his earlier reading of my atom-interferometry alternative (B032): I agree its credit is awkward because of Chu in 1997, and I have therefore dropped it from my alternatives in favour of B057 and B053.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B057 as a new organising principle in condensed matter, argues the 2016 prize concerned model systems and phase transitions whereas Z2 topological band insulators in real materials are distinct, and says the clock is a refinement of precision opened by earlier prizes.
responses.response: His answer to the 2016 overlap is persuasive and I would not use that overlap against B057; I do not think a topology prize is excluded by 2016. Where we still differ is the credit. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are three names for an effect where Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp measured, and I cannot judge it as he can. What would move me to B057 is a reasoned answer from Eriksson and Mehlig that the Kane-Mele proposal and the Molenkamp measurement are sufficiently independent of the HgTe prediction, so that omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (with Zhang deceased) would be defensible and not just convenient. On his novelty point I disagree with calling the lattice clock a refinement. Removing the light shift for neutral atoms in a trap is a change of mechanism, not a better version of the same instrument, and the result is a different regime of precision. He is right that waiting for the second to be redefined would not harm the clock, but I see nothing the committee would gain by waiting, and a risk that the discussion turns to the applications, which is what the prize should not be about. I therefore keep B057 as my first alternative, since I find it the strongest competing science.

responses.point: Mehlig regards B027 as a fully legitimate winner but cautions that a clean credit is partly a consequence of a small number of people on a technique and should not decide the matter on its own.
responses.response: I take that seriously, and I do not want to defend B027 on tidiness. The case rests on the physics: a new mechanism, a new precision regime and independent verification. The clean credit is a bonus that the committee can only rely on if the science is already there, and I think it is. I agree with the point that a small number of names on a technique can make the credit look cleaner than the history of the field, which is why I take Olsson's question about Ye's role as a real one and have written the invention-and-development wording. I note that Mehlig could not make a scientific case against B027 and that the principal remaining differences between us are about weighting a discovery about matter against a measurement capability. That is a legitimate disagreement and I do not think either of us should move merely to match the other.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct mechanism or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes; I think it is distinct but the colleagues who have raised it have not all been persuaded.
Whether Ye's role is stated adequately by invention and development, and whether a wording that more clearly separates Katori's concept from Ye's demonstration would serve better.
Whether the credit for B057 can be defended without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; this is the main thing that would shift my ranking, and I cannot resolve it myself.
Whether the redefinition of the second, expected later this decade, would make a prize now look timely or slightly early.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no collaboration or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and neither my advisor Svanberg nor my postdoc host Aldén is involved. I am on the executive team of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, linked to Chalmers and to Göran Johansson, whose circuit-QED entry (B036) is not in my configuration; he now also places the clock first. My rare-earth quantum-memory work overlaps loosely with B060 and B036 but not with any credited name in my configuration or in my alternatives. My company Deep Light Vision has no connection with any shortlisted candidate. I do not consider any of this a reason for recusal.
